scams.name: Sydney Airport Taxi 'Top-Up' Overcharge Scam
scams.description: You've just landed at Sydney Airport after a 14-hour flight. You skip the Uber queue because the taxi rank looks faster, and a driver waves you over. The meter ticks up to around $48 for the trip into the CBD — reasonable — but as he pulls up to your hotel, he points at the screen and says there's a 'top up' for the airport toll and the late-night rate. Suddenly you're being asked for $85. You're jet-lagged, your bags are in the boot, and you pay just to end it.
scams.avoidance: Your defence is to book a rideshare (Uber, DiDi, Bolt) before you leave the arrivals hall — pickup is at the designated rideshare bay, not the taxi rank. If you must take a taxi, use the official 13cabs or Silver Service app so you have a fare receipt and complaint trail. Always insist on tap-to-pay at the in-car terminal, never hand your card over, and if a driver demands cash or threatens you, take a photo of the taxi licence plate and the driver's ID. As one traveler put it in a 2025 community thread, 'Sydney Taxis are a scam and Uber basically has replaced them for anyone with good sense.' Pre-book Uber, DiDi or Bolt in-app before you clear customs — pickup is at the rideshare bay at T1; If you must take a taxi, use the 13cabs or Silver Service apps so the fare is app-calculated with a receipt; Insist on tap-to-pay at the in-car terminal and watch the terminal — never hand over your physical card; Screenshot the expected fare in Uber before arrival so you know what a legit price looks like (~$45–$60 CBD); If overcharged, pay under protest and file a chargeback with your bank — travelers report Amex disputes succeed
scams.location: Sydney Airport Terminal 1 (international) taxi rank, also T2/T3 domestic

scams.name: Sydney Airport Uber 'Fake Surge' Pricing
scams.description: You open Uber at the rideshare bay expecting a $55 fare to Darlinghurst. The app quotes you $145, flagged as '2.7x surge'. There's no weather, no concert — just a Tuesday afternoon. You wait five minutes, it bumps to $160. You finally accept, and as soon as your ride is confirmed you notice the price drops back to $55 for the next traveller.
scams.avoidance: Your fastest fix is to walk to the public bus stop at T1 and take the 400 bus to Bondi Junction or Mascot station on the T8 line, then catch a train. If you need door-to-door, try DiDi or Bolt instead of Uber — they often have lower surges at SYD since they're less dominant. As one traveler put it on a community surge-pricing thread, 'If the price surges too much, wouldn't people just choose a normal taxi? But yea, pretty devious behavior.' Compare Uber, DiDi and Bolt side-by-side before ordering — one is usually normally priced; Take the airport train from SYD Station (~$22, under 15 min to Central) if you're not jet-lagged; Bus 400 from outside the terminals runs to Bondi Junction for a few dollars; Wait 10 minutes and try again — surges often reset when drivers give up waiting; Pre-book a transfer through your hotel if you're arriving between 11pm–5am when surges are worst
scams.location: Sydney Airport T1 and T2 rideshare pickup bays

scams.name: Fake Short-Stay Rental Listings
scams.description: You've been planning a Sydney trip for months. A studio in Surry Hills pops up on what looks like a legit rental site — $180/night for a week, beautiful photos, the host explains Airbnb fees 'inflate prices' so please bank-transfer direct. You pay $1,260 AUD. When you arrive at the address, the apartment is someone else's home. The 'host' has gone dark.
scams.avoidance: Your defence is bulletproof if you follow two rules. First, always book on airbnb.com or booking.com directly via the app or your browser's known bookmark — never click a link emailed to you. Second, never pay outside the platform. Airbnb's payment system holds your money in escrow and releases it 24 hours after check-in; any host asking you to 'wire to save fees' is scamming you. If you've already paid by bank transfer, call your bank within 24 hours and initiate a recall — some Australian banks can claw back funds if the recipient account hasn't yet withdrawn them. Only open airbnb.com or booking.com via the official app or a bookmarked URL — never a link in email; Pay only inside the platform — Airbnb, Booking.com and Stayz all hold funds in escrow; Reverse image search the listing photos in Google Images before booking; Check the listing has reviews from multiple guests in the past 12 months; If in doubt, phone the actual property via a number you find on Google Maps independently
scams.location: CBD, Surry Hills, Darlinghurst, Bondi — any high-demand Airbnb / Booking.com area

scams.name: Bondi / Manly Beach Bag & Phone Theft
scams.description: You've dreamed about swimming at Bondi your whole life. You walk down from the promenade, drop your backpack on a towel, leave your phone on top — 'Aussies are friendly, nobody steals' — and go in for a swim. Fifteen minutes later your bag is still there, but the phone, wallet and passport inside are gone.
scams.avoidance: Your defences are three-fold. Use the paid lockers at Bondi Pavilion (around $5–10, opposite the main beach). Take a waterproof phone pouch into the water and leave nothing visible on the sand. Or go to the beach in shifts with a travel partner — one swims while the other minds the bags. The best NSW Police advice, echoed in traveler communities, is the same as for any beach worldwide: the less your bag looks like a tourist bag, the less likely it is to be picked. Leave your passport at the hotel safe and bring only a bank card, a photocopy of your passport, and enough cash for food. Use the paid lockers at Bondi Pavilion, Manly Surf Club or Coogee Pavilion; Take a waterproof pouch (Aquapac, SealLine) into the water with phone, card and key; Go to the beach in shifts — one person stays with the bags at all times; Leave your passport in the hotel safe; carry a photocopy plus one bank card; Use a $20 drybag with a carabiner, not an obvious tourist backpack
scams.location: Bondi Beach, Manly Beach, Coogee Beach — sand in front of the surf clubs

scams.name: Opal Card & Fare Confusion Trap
scams.description: You land at Sydney Airport and head to the train platform. A friendly-looking person at the ticket machine 'helps' you buy a $22 single-use paper ticket because it's easier — except a contactless tap on your bank card is $15.94, and an Opal card would cap your day at $18. Over a week in Sydney, that difference adds up to $60–$100 lost on fares.
scams.avoidance: Your approach is simple. Link your contactless bank card (Visa, Mastercard, Amex debit or credit) to the Opal reader — it's automatic, caps at $18.40 weekdays and $8.40 weekends (2026 rates), and works on train, bus, ferry, light rail. Always tap BOTH on and off, even on buses where there's no gate. Download the free Opal Travel app to see your trip history so you can catch any max-fare mis-taps immediately and claim a refund at a staffed station. Tap on and off with your contactless bank card — it's automatic, no Opal card needed; If your card isn't contactless-compatible, buy an Opal card at any convenience store; ALWAYS tap both on AND off — this is the single most common mistake tourists make; Download the Opal Travel app to track your balance and trip history in real time; Request uniform ID from any 'inspector' — Transport NSW staff wear clearly branded uniforms
scams.location: Sydney Airport station, Central Station, Circular Quay ferry wharves

scams.name: Counterfeit BridgeClimb, Vivid & Opera House Ticket Scam
scams.description: You're walking near Cumberland Street at dusk and a man with a printed ticket approaches you. BridgeClimb Sydney at $170–$335 has felt expensive all trip, and he's offering the 'Twilight Climb' tonight at $80 off because 'my mate's a guide and a tourist cancelled.' He sends you a QR code on WhatsApp. You pay in cash. At the BridgeClimb reception, the QR is invalid, his WhatsApp is a dead number, and tonight's climb is sold out anyway.
scams.avoidance: The 'offer comes to you' heuristic is your best filter. If you discovered the ticket yourself on the official site, it's legitimate. If a stranger, a DM, or a Facebook ad is offering you a discount, it's almost certainly fraud. Book premium Sydney experiences 2–4 weeks in advance through official sites — hotel concierges also have real agreements with some operators and can save you 5–15% transparently. Book BridgeClimb at bridgeclimb.com and Opera House events at sydneyoperahouse.com only; For Vivid Sydney, use the official vividsydney.com programme and Opera House channels; Ignore any 'discount ticket' DM, Facebook ad or street offer — there are no legitimate resellers; Pay by credit card for chargeback protection — never bank transfer or cash for tickets; Ask your hotel concierge about genuine discount partnerships (they exist but require hotel booking)
scams.location: The Rocks, Circular Quay, Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree
